name: Retinol

lead: Retinol is a form of vitamin A (an alcohol) used in over-the-counter serums and creams for fine lines, uneven tone and rough texture. It is one of the most common anti-aging cosmetic ingredients and is often positioned as a gentler step toward prescription retinoids.

Evidence for improvement in photoaged skin exists in clinical studies and reviews, but results are generally slower and milder than with tretinoin, and product concentration, formulation stability and packaging heavily influence real-world performance.

paras: After it enters the skin, retinol is oxidized in two enzymatic steps to retinaldehyde and then to retinoic acid, which activates retinoic acid receptors and alters gene expression. The downstream effects are increased epidermal turnover, greater collagen production and less breakdown of existing collagen. Because conversion is limited and inefficient, the amount of retinoic acid generated is small, which explains both its milder effect and its better tolerability.

Dryness, redness, flaking and photosensitivity are the usual side effects and tend to ease with gradual introduction and moisturizer. Retinol is oxidation- and light-sensitive, so poorly formulated products may lose potency. Dermatology guidance generally advises avoiding topical retinoids during pregnancy as a precaution. It is sold without prescription but concentrations are regulated in some regions.
